entry.title: Winterize Your Bed and Bath Setup at Brooklinen’s Sale
entry.summary: From sheets to towels to robes.
entry.content:
The clocks are turning back, the weather is cooling off — it’s time to get your bedding and bath winter-ready. A ton of Brooklinen’s excellent sheets, pillowcases, duvets, and more are currently (and conveniently) on sale for the brand’s friends and family sale. Sitewide, all items are 20 percent off, but bundles are up to 50 percent off. There’s a lot in the sale section, so I culled through our best-of-brand roundup to find the best deals this time around. The discount code should apply automatically, but if not, it’s FRIENDSANDFAM.

As always, make sure to sign up for the Strategist Deal Freaks Daily newsletter to receive each day’s best deals in your inbox (as well as sales just for newsletter subscribers). And if you want even more, sign up for our regular email newsletter for tons more newsletter exclusives.

One of the best discounts in the sale is on this nice duvet cover and two matching shams. It’s made from a mix of cotton and linen, which keeps it feeling crisp yet soft. And the walnut-brown shade is gorgeous for winter — but there’s also ecru and umber colorways.

Linen is a good temperature regulator, making these sheets ideal for all seasons. In the winter, they feel really cozy and soft — Strategist lead editor Lauren Levy said they made her “fall in love with linen sheets.” This bundle is a great deal because it includes matching flat and fitted sheets plus four pillowcases and a duvet cover. It’s currently available in eight solid neutrals, 14 stripes, three checks, and one floral pattern.

For seriously warm sheets, flannel is your best friend. The bundle will fully make over your bed, but you can also get just the sheets or pillowcases for 20 percent off.

Our Best in Class sateen sheets are silky and substantial, made from cotton with a 480 thread count. “It is really hard to beat the quality of these sheets for the price,” interior designer Molly Schoneveld told us. “They feel like butter and still look and feel great after many times in the wash.” The sheet sets are currently 20 percent off; the bundle (which includes a flat sheet, a fitted sheet, four pillowcases, and a duvet cover) is 35 percent off.

If you want to replace your comforter for the cold weather, this one comes in a heavyweight version filled with certified Canadian down. “If you prefer a low-maintenance down comforter — a.k.a. one that doesn’t require constant fluffing — this one is for you,” says Strategist bedding expert Lauren Ro.

Add an extra blanket to your bed while you’re at it. This one is made with a 100 percent cotton shell and has hand-stitched detailing.

Our favorite down pillow for neck support. “If you love plush and squishy hotel pillows but wish they had a smidge more neck support, the Brooklinen down could be a match for you,” says our sleep writer, Amelia Jerden. You can choose between soft, medium, and firm.

If you want warm, soft bedding, this will feel super luxurious on your skin. Also available in sheets, a duvet cover, and the full bundle for 35 percent off.

A silk pillowcase (especially on sale) is always a good bet, no matter the season. This one is available in ten colors and patterns and will keep your hair and skin so smooth while you sleep.

Here’s a good gift or stocking stuffer at an especially great price. “It’s soft, slightly larger than the Slip mask, and loose enough that it doesn’t give me headaches despite not having an adjustable strap,” says Strategist writer Bella Druckman. “It’s the perfect size to throw in my carry-on before a flight.” And it’s a lot cheaper than other status-y sleep masks.

Our favorite heavyweight bath towels are currently on sale — the bundle of two bath towels and two hand towels is 30 percent off. They’re incredibly thick and absorbent (ideal for coming out of the shower in a cold apartment) and also feel indulgent, according to Ro.

One of the best deals of the whole sale is on this waffle-weave bundle (two bath towels and two hand towels), which is available in nine colors and patterns.

There’s nothing like a cozy robe in the cold weather. This one is our best all-around bathrobe, according to Strategist writer Ambar Pardilla, because it’s comfortable, soft, and absorbent. It’s another great gift option and is available in nine really lovely striped colorways.

entry.title: Everything I Used to Run-Commute to an Office With No Showers for a Week (Again)
entry.summary: The goal was to run as unencumbered as possible.
entry.content:
The lore of my middle-school track team goes like this: Years before our time, there was a very fast runner named Greg on the team. On the days of a meet, if Greg didn’t win his race, he would run home instead of taking the bus or catching a ride.

I don’t know if Greg actually existed or whether his run home was enforced by his parents or self-inflicted in a relatable Catholic way, but I have been thinking about his run commute ever since I learned about him.

In 2024, partly inspired by Greg and as a way to increase my weekly mileage for fall marathon training, I ran to and from the office for a week straight. Not much has changed since then: I still live in the same Brooklyn apartment, I’m training for the New York City Marathon again, the offices of New York are still in the Financial District, and, most important, they still don’t have showers.

Two years later, I sought to run-commute for another week, but I didn’t want to bring my laptop or any office items with me this time — I wanted to carry as little as possible. I would still freshen up and makeshift “shower” in the bathrooms as best I could, but a secret goal was to do it all discreetly, to make my run undetectable.

My apartment is just under four miles from the office. I don’t have anything with me except my phone, keys, and building security card. Yesterday was a company holiday, so to prepare for the runs this week, last night I dropped off a haul of items at the office: four outfits, a pair of work-appropriate shoes, a few meal-prepped lunches, toiletries, and towels, all of which fit inside my On Track Pack with ease.

I run across the Manhattan Bridge and then head south toward Wall Street. It takes me just under half an hour, and I show up drenched in sweat. It’s much more humid this year compared with two years ago.

I packed more than I would for a short vacation, but the more substantial drop-off was crucial: In addition to body wipes, I have actual face wash and body and face towels to dry off, as well as a toothbrush and razor.

After work, I run across the Williamsburg Bridge back into Brooklyn to meet my friend Grace for pizza. I run into my friend Rowan at an ice-cream shop afterward, and we briefly catch up. He says I positively do not smell, which is reaffirming.

Back home, it’s nice not to have subtle reminders of the office, like my laptop and planner, on my desk. It reminds me of how it felt to turn off my phone for a while this winter: Work is left at work. Adding the ten miles I ran yesterday, I’m at 18 miles this week.

Daily mileage: 8.52 miles
Weekly mileage: 18.67 miles

As I run toward the Manhattan Bridge, I find someone’s passport on the street. When I get to the office, I look him up and reach out. We make plans to coordinate a handoff in the evening.

I don’t normally run with my phone. (My hot take is that no running-apparel brand has successfully made clothing that can carry a phone well.) But tucking it into the back pocket of my half-tights has proved to be the easiest option; most running shorts lack a compressive enough waistband or pocket to prevent the contents from flopping around.

To prevent my two keys from jangling, I wrap them in Velcro garden ties before each run and stash them in a plastic ID holder where I keep my cards and my lucky Pokémon card, which I take along on every run.

Drying my running clothes from the morning session is a challenge I didn’t have the last time I did this experiment (the weather that week was cool and dry; today it’s 65 degrees and humid). As I prepare for my run home, I realize my shirt is still a bit damp. Next time, I’ll bring extra running clothes.

I meet the passport guy outside a Raising Cane’s Chicken Fingers, and he offers to buy me some as a thank-you. I politely decline. I trust there will be more karmic chicken fingers in my future.

Daily mileage: 7.6 miles
Weekly mileage: 26.27 miles 

My legs feel a bit tired. I’m training for my fourth marathon in two years, and my previous training blocks haven’t incorporated many double sessions (a run in the morning, then again later in the day). But with my peak-mileage weeks behind me, I try to keep the bulk of these runs light and easy. I make sure to rotate my shoes throughout the week: My daily driver pair for the most easy running (Asics Megablast and New Balance SuperComp Rebel V1), a more responsive pair for track workouts and interval training and the shoe I plan to use for the marathon (On Cloudboom Strike 2), and then a max-cushion shoe for recovery days (Asics Slowcush).

Coincidentally, earlier this week a brand called Zip Running reached out to me asking if I wanted to test its packs, which are made specifically for run-commuting. They sent me two, and I decided to test the smaller one, the FKC, for tonight’s run home.

On the way, I decide to go uptown to the Empire State Building. It’s one of those tourist attractions I never got around to visiting, but I’ve always wanted to see the view from the observation deck. The FKC pack’s shoulder straps fit snugly across my chest, like a trail-running vest. I don’t have much inside — just a hat, water bottle, T-shirt, and packet of Welch’s Fruit Snacks.

The exterior has the shiny, durable finish of a Patagonia Black Hole backpack, but the TPU-coated polyester is much lighter than those travel-specific packs. The bungee-cord straps cinch securely across my chest, and there’s no bounce. I don’t feel it impacting my stride or form at all, but I can imagine that might not be the case with a heavier load like a laptop.

The view from 86 floors above Manhattan is incredible. I stay for half an hour before running home across the Manhattan Bridge once more.

Daily mileage: 8.40 miles 
Weekly mileage: 34.67 miles

On average, it has taken me about 30 minutes to run to the office each day this week. Normally, it takes me 25 to 30 minutes to commute via train, door-to-door and with no MTA delays. I realize I’m not saving much time, but the view from the bridge makes it worth it.

My colleague Jacob regularly run-commutes to the office too. His trick is that he showers at a gym near the office and keeps a change of shoes (both running shoes and work-appropriate pairs) in his desk drawer. He tested the larger Zip running pack on his commute today.

“I ran about nine or so miles with it and found it comfy the whole time,” he says, adding that the backpack rides really well with its bungee-cord-like system (as opposed to buckles). Much like the smaller version of the pack I tested, this one sits higher up on the back, which Jacob also appreciated. “Usually, I have a big problem with backpacks messing up my shirt, and I find that a raw piece of plastic has eviscerated my lower back into a chafe that my girlfriend calls ‘the red scar.’ And I sort of half scream in the shower after running. Today: no screaming,” he says.

I pack up the things I’ve left at the office for the week and head home.

Daily mileage: 3.84 miles
Weekly mileage: 38.51 miles

It’s the weekend. While these aren’t run-commute days, I realize I’m carrying more with me on these longer weekend runs than during the week because of my various gels and fuel. I’ve changed my fueling significantly over the past two years and started having simply more carbs before and during my runs.

My favorite gels are the GU Liquid Energy, which is more drinkable than a typical thicker gel. I like that I don’t have to take these with water, and that comes in handy especially during races. But sometimes my stomach agrees with something a little more solid, in which case I’ll pack some Gu Salted Lime and Precision Fuel gels.

When snacking throughout the day, I like to have PB&Js and yogurt and granola, but when I have to eat quickly before a run, I like these SaltStick sour gummies, which have more sodium than a typical gummy snack. I’ve also found Trader Joe’s fruit crushers (which are really just applesauce) have a decent amount of carbs per packet (16 grams), about half the amount you’ll find in a typical gel.

This weekend, I do an easy ten-miler and then a 14-mile run with some marathon-pace miles thrown in the middle. It’s my final long run before race day in two weeks.

Weekend mileage: 24.3 miles
Weekly mileage: 62.81 miles

It’s a new week. Without the beginning-of-the-week haul, this is my first day of bringing everything I need with me on my run (minus the laptop, which I left at the office over the weekend). I pack a change of clothes into the FKC pack: a shirt, pants, underwear, socks, and loafers (which, surprisingly, are my lightest pair of shoes). When I get to the office, one of my co-workers asks if I ran here today. I tell her I run-commuted all of last week; she tells me she didn’t even notice. Before I run home, I leave my work laptop at the office. I plan to keep it here all week.

Daily mileage: 7.54 miles
Total mileage: 70.35 miles

entry.title: This Year, All the Teens Want a Wavytalk Thermal Brush
entry.summary: They’re using it to create bouncy blowouts at home.
entry.content:
Every year, there’s a buzzy new product that every teenage girl puts on her holiday wish list. Last year, it was all about Rhode (specifically, the Peptide Lip Tint). The year before that, we saw the rise (and fall) of White Fox sweatshirts. And the year before that, it was Stanley tumblers. There are always some hair tools in the mix, too, and while it’s usually the Dyson AirWrap and Shark gadgets that get the “Most Wanted” asterisk on the list, this year it seems there’s a new (to teens) contender: the Wavytalk blowout brush.

Founded in 2021 as an affordable option for at-home hairstyling, Waytalk has since made cheaper versions of every hair tool on the spectrum, from a $219 version of the AirWrap to a $60 hair-crimping iron. In 2024, the brand became the official hair-tool sponsor of Sabrina Carpenter’s Short n’ Sweet Tour, and it has only continued to grow. In the last year or so, it has expanded into skin-care devices, with a $100 LED mask and $279 micro-current device, and it even made its own heat protectant. Still, nothing seems capable of overshadowing the blowout brush, which turned the brand into a household name — or, at least, a high-school-hallway name.

The brush comes in two versions, a 1.5-inch and 1.75-inch barrel, which are ideal for short-to-medium hair and medium-to-long hair, respectively. They’re especially popular on TikTok Shop where, at the time of writing, Wavytalk has sold 1.4 million of the 1.5-inch brushes. Over the past several months, the thermal brush has been coming up in my conversations with teens, and I’ve noticed it climbing on the “Top 100 Trending” list on Giftful, Gen Z’s favorite wish-list-making app. I’ve been curious to see if the brush is actually worth the hype, so I put it to the test. My honest thoughts, below.

Each box includes the device itself along with two solidly mediocre hair clips for heat styling. If you’re planning to gift this to someone, I recommend adding on a claw clip or other hair sectioning clip with more grip.

I tried both sizes of the thermal brush, but I found the 1.75-inch version worked best on my medium-length, medium-textured hair. It takes more patience than other pricier thermal brushes I’ve tried, like my go-to brush from Calista, but I haven’t found a better thermal brush for the price than the Wavytalk.

With patience, it delivers a sleek, bouncy blowout, but its most impressive feature is decreasing frizz thanks to the brush’s negative ion technology. Ionic stylers like these emit negative ions to seal the hair cuticle, which makes thicker hair look sleek, and thinner hair lose its body, according to our beauty writer, Krista Bennett DeMaio. My hair naturally dries wavy with some frizz, and no matter how carefully I blow out my hair with my Shark FlexStyle or T3 hair dryer, I can never seem to tame the frizz completely. When I use the Wavytalk, though, all that frizz disappears for at least 24 hours — or until I wash my hair. Since my hair isn’t quite thick or thin, I haven’t had any trouble maintaining volume either.

It’s worth noting that you should dry your hair before using the thermal brush, which doesn’t blow out hot air like a blow-dryer brush. (Air drying and heat drying are both fine.) Instead, the brush heats the bristles and ceramic barrel to one of five temperatures that range from 300 to 420 degrees. Wavytalk recommends using the 360- or 390-degree settings on wavy hair like mine, but I’ve been preferring the latter, which helps my stubbornish hair better hold the loose curl the brush creates. The Wavytalk is most effective when working with small sections of hair, so I recommend working from the bottom up with two or three inches’ worth of hair at a time. Small sections like these prevent hair from getting tangled around the brush. It also helps create stronger curls that pop with the help of my layers.

While styling each section, I typically go through three steps. First, I put the brush underneath the section and rotate it while moving outward (as in, away from my head). Then I’ll put the brush on top of the hair and repeat the same motion. These two steps typically eliminate any frizz and waviness from my hair while the next step is when the actual curl happens. To get the bounce in your bouncy blowout, you’ll want to place the brush below the section again, brush it out to the end, and roll it inward, so all the hair is wrapped around the brush. Then I’ll hold it for 10 to 15 seconds and spray some hair spray if I’m looking for more pronounced curls. There are plenty of tutorials online for tweens and teens learning how to style their hair for the first time, but the learning curve is relatively small.

If your teen already has, say, a Dyson AirWrap or Shark FlexStyle, they probably don’t need a Wavytalk. But if they’re a hair newbie asking for a Dyson or a Shark, I’d recommend getting them a Wavytalk brush instead. When you factor in heat protectants and hair sprays, learning how to style your hair is an expensive journey, and it’s best to start with an affordable heat tool during the learning process — especially if you’re only planning to use it every once in a while. The Wavytalk is ideal for figuring out the basics, like creating a curl and giving your hair volume. And for girls with frizzy hair like me, it’s a quick way to make your hair shine before a long day in the classroom. I wish I had a tool like this when I was in high school.

entry.title: The Strategist Readers Choice’ Award Winners
entry.summary: Thousands of you cast hundreds of thousands of votes to crown some of the best products we’ve written about over the past ten years.
entry.content:
Over the course of a decade, we’ve tried a lot of stuff. Our intrepid team of Strategist staffers has spent years testing, researching, consulting experts, and debating with one another about which products within the vast online-shopping landscape, from mattresses to moisturizers, are actually worth your money. The result is a thoroughly vetted compendium of Best in Class nail clippers and underwear; fugly shoes that are comfortable for miles and miles; and the weirdest, most useful doodads money can buy.

But throughout these ten years, our readers have been buying and trying out things right alongside us, and they’ve got thoughts to share. We asked them to decide which of our already cherry-picked favorites should be crowned the absolute crème de la crème. Back in July, we put out a call for responses to our first Readers’ Choice poll, asking participants to choose their favorite products in 47 categories. Thousands of people cast hundreds of thousands of votes, and after we tallied everything up, the products below emerged as the winners. Below, we present the pick of the litter in dozens of categories, including beauty, fashion, kitchen, travel, and more.

At least seven dermatologists have recommended this CeraVe cleanser to us. That plus its affordable price and drugstore availability is why it’s long been our top face wash for oily skin.

Runner-up: Cetaphil Gentle Skin Cleanser

Strategist contributor Rio Viera-Newton praised Nécessaire’s pH-balanced bodywash for its thick, honeylike texture and elevated scent.

Runner-up: Dove Foaming Body Wash

It’s frills-free, but it works. That’s why derms recommend La Roche-Posay’s moisturizer for both teen and mature skin.

Runner-up: CeraVe Moisturizing Cream

The SkinCeuticals vitamin-C serum is admittedly pricey, but there’s a reason it’s garnered such a devoted following. The formula is highly potent without causing irritation and counts beauty scientists and dermatologists among its many fans. Our own writer Tembe Denton-Hurst has been using it for several years: “I’d rather spend close to $200 on a vitamin C I know is going to work than waste money on less expensive products that may or not be doing their job,” she says.

Runner-up: CeraVe Skin Renewing Vitamin C Serum

For those with oily and acne-prone skin, Differin is still king. You’ll find it in the medicine cabinets of teens, dermatologists, and beauty writers alike.

Runner-up: RoC Retinol Correxion Line Smoothing Eye Cream

A truly excellent drugstore mascara that creates lots of length and volume. “They make your eyelashes ten times longer and darker,” Skai Jackson told us.

Runner-up: L’Oréal Voluminous Waterproof Mascara

Celebrities, Strategist staffers, and our loyal readers all agree: The Laneige sleeping mask is an all-time-great lip product.

Runner-up: Clinique Black Honey

The Dyson Supersonic is still the gold standard for hair dryers, reliably appearing on Christmas wish lists every December. It’s a favorite of three Strategist writers, all of whom have very different hair types.

Runner-up: Remington Damage Protection Hair Dryer

The Shark CryoGlow mask kept one writer’s skin so smooth and breakout-free it got a compliment from her dad.

Runner-up: CurrentBody LED Light Mask

A callus-smoothing “podiatric miracle” product that’s been a best seller on our site for ten years and counting.

Runner-up: O’Keeffe’s Foot Cream

We’re big fans of Uniqlo’s wardrobe basics here at the Strategist, and its white tee is no exception. The U Crew T-shirt is our pick for the best less-expensive white T-shirt because it’s got a thicker, heavyweight feel to it that won’t put your bra on display.

Runner-up: Old Navy EveryWear Crop T-Shirt

The humble Hanes tee is a tried-and-true classic. It has a nice medium-weight feel but also comes in affordable three-packs, so no need to feel too bad if they get stained or dirty.

Runner-up: Uniqlo Supima Cotton T-Shirt

One stylist we spoke to said she’s recommended Madewell’s Perfect Vintage jeans to over 150 clients.

Runner-up: Levi’s 501 Original-Fit Jeans

We can’t resist a trompe l’oeil moment, especially if it means our pants look like jeans but feel like sweatpants. In fact, Strategist writer Brenley Goertzen loves Rag & Bone’s Miramar collection so much that she owns five different pairs.

Runner-up: Le Bon Shoppe Arc Pants

There was a time when Strategist writer Ambar Pardilla wore Banana Republic Hayden work pants to an office nearly every day. “Despite my commute, which included a car ride, a trip on New Jersey Transit, some subway stops, and a few blocks on foot, the pants always made it to the office unwrinkled,” she says.

Runner-up: Aritzia Effortless Pant

Few brands are as closely associated with the word crewneck as Champion. Chris Black says its sweatshirts are “not fussy, just roomy and warm.”

Runner-up: Hanes EcoSmart Fleece Sweatshirt

Comfortable, sturdy, soft, and seamless: all reasons why we declared Natori’s Bliss Girl Briefs the best brief. Readers love them too — they’re an all-time Strategist best seller.

Runner-up: Gap Organic Stretch Cotton Hipster

Boxer briefs blend the support of briefs with the length of traditional boxers — and the logo-patterned Calvin Klein waistband is pretty iconic to boot.

Runner-up: J.Crew Cotton Boxers

Viera-Newton decided to buy this Skims bralette thanks to the vouching of her “bra snob” friends. It also has a one of the largest size ranges we’ve seen: XXS to 4X.

Runner-up: Lane Bryant Comfort Bliss No-Wire Lounge Bra

Dansko clogs are one of the original fugly shoes that has come to define the Strategist. They’re worn by restaurant workers, hospital staff, pregnant people, and even Zendaya.

Runner-up: Merrell Jungle Moc

At this point, everyone and their mother likely owns an Away carry-on. It’s been recommended to us by travel experts time and time (and time) again.

Runner-up: Travelpro VersaPack+ Lightweight Softside Expandable Carry-on Luggage

When the Strategist team debated the merits of L.L.Bean’s Boat and Tote versus the Lands’ End tote bag, many argued in favor of the Boat and Tote for its stiff, durable canvas; capacious design; and classic monogrammed look. Strategist readers agree.

Runner-up: Lands’ End Medium 5-Pocket Open-Top Canvas Tote Bag

Our travel writer describes the Trtl Travel Pillow as “a scarf crossed with an Elizabethan collar.” It’s such a ubiquitous favorite that, in addition to earning a spot our Best in Class Hall of Fame, it’s also in our Travel Hall of Fame and our Sleep Hall of Fame.

Runner-up: Coop Sleep Goods Airjustable Travel Neck Pillow

Our long-running favorite mattress from Saatva will keep just about anyone cozy with a nice balance of support and comfort.

Runner-up: Leesa Original Hybrid Mattress

Our best overall pillow suits pretty much any sort of sleeper since you can adjust the amount of fill inside — and it’s priced under $100.

Runner-up: Beckham Hotel Collection Down Alternative Pillow

ICYMI: Target’s in-house Threshold line makes some of the best affordable sateen sheets out there. They come in a nice range of colors and patterns and have a surprisingly substantial feel relative to their price tag.

Runner-up: Brooklinen Luxe Sateen Core Sheet Set

Placebo or real? Either way, it’s working: Using this spray on her feet before bed helped Strategist contributor Diksha Basu reliably fall asleep within minutes, inspiring thousands of Strategist readers to try it too.

Runner-up: Scentered Lavender Aromatherapy Balm Stick

Whether you’re recovering from intense workouts or you’re just an achy person, Hyperice’s Hypervolt 3 is our fitness writer’s most-used massage gun for relieving deep-tissue soreness.

Runner-up: TriggerPoint GRID 1.0 Foam Roller

The Owala FreeSip is a popular sight among Strategist staffers — 11 of us owned it back in 2023, and it’s still going strong.

Runner-up: Hydro Flask 24-Oz. Standard-Mouth Water Bottle

In New York apartment kitchens, single-use gadgets need to earn their place. The OXO julienne peeler does just that. Senior kitchen and dining writer Emma Wartzman uses it more than she ever expected she would to shred carrots, zucchini, and more into uniform strips that are delightful to eat.

Runner-up: Chef’n Cob Corn Stripper

Here at the Strategist, we appreciate the very best version of a utilitarian item. When it comes to spatulas, it’s GIR’s silicone one — it doesn’t peel, warp, bend, or pick up smells.

Runner-up: Stasher Sandwich Bag

Vitamix has a lot of blenders, but multiple cooks and food-industry professionals have told us they prefer the 750 for its sharp blades and powerful motor. With it, making soups and smoothies is a breeze.

Runner-up: Cuisinart Smart Stick Variable Speed Blender

Bialetti’s moka pot is a classic Italian espresso machine that looks very handsome on your stovetop. Plus it’s a tool that Isabella Rossellini can’t live without — she uses it to make two espressos a day.

Runner-up: Bonavita 8-Cup Coffee Maker

We’ve tested enough Dyson vacuums to know that pretty much any model you get will be high-powered enough to quickly suck up every last bit of dust, dirt, and hair. Based on our survey results, Strategist readers are on the same page.

Runner-up: Shark PowerDetect Cordless Vacuum Clean and Empty System

A spot cleaner that’s portable, compact, and delightfully designed, described by writer Erin Schwartz as “a Shop-Vac with a shampoo trigger.”

Runner-up: SonicScrubber

Brooklinen’s bath towels are hefty: Our home writer says they are “extremely thick and sumptuous” and “absorb water quickly and efficiently” post-shower.

Runner-up: Lands’ End Premium Supima Cotton Bath Towel Set

Ikea’s moody globe-shaped lamp is a favorite among the designers and creative types we’ve talked to because it’s simple, inconspicuous, and stylish. Pop a color-changing lightbulb inside for best results.

Runner-up: Anglepoise Type 75 Desk Lamp

After sitting on 99 couches, our couch expert kept coming back to this one from Crate & Barrel because it is customizable and reasonably priced and boasts some of the comfiest seat cushions they’ve tried.

Runner-up: Article Hanson Sofa

entry.title: I Snipped and Sliced With 10 Pairs of Kitchen Shears. These Are the Best.
entry.summary: For prepping herbs, spatchcocking chicken, trimming flowers, and so much more.
entry.content:
Knives tend to get all the glory when it comes to kitchen cutting tasks, but I pick up kitchen shears multiple times a day, every day. I use them to snip herbs, like separating parsley leaves from their stems or chopping chives. I use them to cut chunks of meat for recipes that require bite-size pieces. And while I’m not one to break down my own meat and fish unless I’m in a bind (I usually ask my butcher), you can use kitchen shears to spatchcock a chicken, debone chicken parts, and cut through seafood shells or fins. If you have the right pair, it’s easier than you might think. Kitchen shears are good for vegetable prep, like trimming green beans, or removing the tough stems from mushrooms. You can use them to trim pie or pastry dough. And then, of course, I regularly cut all kinds of nonedible (but kitchen-related) things: fresh flowers, twine, the rubber bands placed around bundles of produce, parchment paper, packages of food, and masking tape for labeling. Kitchen shears are pretty indispensable.

Still, not all are created equal, so I set out to find the best of the best. To start: I consulted the Best in Class guide one of our contributors wrote a few years ago, and then did some additional research, pulling a handful more models from trusted brands. There are a few different styles: mostly larger pull-apart scissors, a couple of larger ones that don’t detach, and a couple of small attached ones (like the classic Joyce Chen model). I wasn’t too scientific about my selection: I simply called in whatever spoke to me.

The first thing I did was pick up, hold, and examine each pair. This gave me an initial inkling of preference. How scissors feel in your hand is important. Then, where possible, I took the two sides apart. I don’t always do this to clean — only when a task is particularly gnarly — but being able to separate with ease, as well as making sure the pieces stay in place when in use, is definitely an important consideration.

Then I used each of them to do a handful of the nonedible tasks I laid out above, testing how smoothly each pair opened and closed, as well as how easily they sliced through some of those materials. This alone allowed me to eliminate a few.

I was surprised to find that these weren’t my favorite. I love Messermeister’s knives — and a different style of its scissors, below. While the edges are sharp, and I like the push-button mechanism that separates the sides, opening and closing them while cutting is decidedly sticky, and they feel a bit heavy in my smaller-size hand. Especially when taking price into consideration, I’d personally pass (though I did also try this similar but smaller collaboration version made with Esther Choi, which I like a bit better thanks to the size).

Again, both of these cut fine, but I don’t love the way either feels to hold. The OXO shears are arguably worse: Like the Messermeister pair, they’re a bit sticky. But even more notably, the handle material is particularly cheap. Though I didn’t have such a negative visceral reaction to the Cangshan ones, I just found them to be somewhat clunky overall.

I really wanted to love these. Clearly, a lot of thought went into designing them: They operate with a spring mechanism that has the blades separated when unlocked, until you press them together to cut (basically the opposite of other shears). Milk Street primarily touts their ability to tackle “big jobs” like spatchcocking a chicken, though it also says they’re precise enough to snip chives. At the end of the day, they’re supremely heavy-duty — so much so that I found them inconvenient to use, especially for smaller tasks. I did cut through chicken bones with them and broke down some cardboard boxes, too. But I found them awkward and difficult to grip. If you’re one to do a lot of butchering, I could maybe see keeping these around, but I’d never pull them out for daily tasks.

From there, I simply started to use the remaining ones in the course of my everyday cooking. I cut chunks of steak for stir-fry and fried rice and snipped long strips of bacon for carbonara. I trimmed herbs, shelled shrimp, separated big grape clusters into smaller ones, and cut slices of kale directly into a simmering pot of soup. All along, I took care to alternate between the scissors and to notice when I began regularly gravitating toward any in particular.

I’ve used Joyce Chen’s classic scissors for years, and they work incredibly well. They’re sharp enough to handle tougher tasks, and they last a decently long time. I was, in fact, surprised to find that I liked another Messermeister pair in the same style better, which is the reason Joyce Chen’s got relegated to this section. The blades here are shorter (but not to the point where I found them to be more precise), the handle is not quite as comfortable, and the open-and-close movement isn’t quite as smooth. I will say these are all details I clocked when directly comparing, and they were not particularly noticeable when using the Joyce Chen pair on its own.

These are one of two pairs I tested that don’t come apart. I like them, but slightly prefer the Zwilling pair I detail below. Side by side, these are just not as smooth and lightweight — though I certainly wouldn’t be mad to have them in my arsenal.

I think it’s nice that these come in two sizes, and they both work very well. I’m especially a fan of the smaller ones, which are somewhat of a hybrid between a classic bigger style and the small-bladed, large-handled Joyce Chen and Messermeister models. If you have more petite hands, that pair fits well.

Finally, I spent even more time cooking with my few favorites, the true standouts — all of which I love for different reasons and will keep in rotation.

These don’t come apart for cleaning, but they’ve become my own go-to for a lot of those nonedible tasks I mentioned up top. They’re really sharp, lightweight, and comfortable — and honestly, I’ve just found myself reaching for them a bunch on instinct. And they’re cheap, so I won’t care if they degrade over time (a definite eventual outcome with tasks like breaking down boxes, which I do a lot of).

This is the pair that I felt had a slight edge over the Joyce Chen shears. The handles are rounder and plumper, such that they’re comfortable to hold. The blades are a tad longer, which helps cut quickly — though they’re still small enough to be exacting when necessary. And they maneuver especially smoothly, with no resistance whatsoever.

These are my true favorites. The blade length is right around the same size as the smaller Misen. The handle, however, is longer, thanks to an opening in the middle with steel-tooth insets to twist off bottle and jar caps. They’re an incredibly durable pair, the only one on this list made entirely from stainless steel. All the others have plastic handles. Still, they’re not as heavy or bulky as I anticipated. Indeed, they’re quite elegant-looking. I love the way they feel in my hand and the way they cut: confidently and precisely.

entry.title: The iPhone Duo Is Pricey and Inconvenient, But I Love This Freaky Little Thing
entry.summary: It’s impressive, if imperfect.
entry.content:
I have been an iPad user since the very beginning — I used my bar mitzvah money to purchase the first-generation device — but I switched to the iPad mini when it came out in 2012, and I currently own the seventh-generation version of that. Judge me all you want, but it is, in my opinion, the ideal piece of technology. It’s separate enough from my computer that I don’t feel stressed when I use it; it’s meaningfully more engaging than my phone because of the larger, more engrossing screen; and it’s small enough that I could theoretically plop it in my tote bag and bring it with me around the city. The issue is, I don’t do that. I have wasted many minutes leaving the house, toiling over whether it’s worth adding that tiny bit of extra weight to my already-heavy bag just to possibly whip out my iPad on the subway for 15 minutes and then have to deal with the social anxiety of being such a public iPad person. So my beloved iPad mini mostly stays at home. But when rumors began swirling of a foldable iPhone that would open up to a size similar to the iPad mini, I felt a tug on my heartstrings. In the time since the iPhone Duo was announced, I’ve used my mini with a wistfulness, like a parent spending a final summer with their child before sending them off to college. Was I really going to abandon my beloved iPad mini for this new device? For the past week, I’ve done just that. And unfortunately, I love this freaky little thing.

I wasn’t immediately smitten. It’s a big adjustment. The front screen of the device is shorter and wider — often described as passport size, but as someone who is still waiting for his new license in the mail and has been forced to carry around his passport, I can tell you it’s smaller than that. A better comparison is BlackBerry size, which feels fitting: While the one-handed typing experience is worse than on a regular iPhone, the two-thumb experience is much more satisfying, like sending a BBM in the good old days.

The software has been reworked for the asymmetrical display, putting the controls on the right side while attempting to maintain a decent amount of vertical space to re-create the typical iPhone experience. For apps that have not been updated to fill the Duo’s screens (and most of them have not at the time of this writing — and maybe never will), the experience on the front screen is quite small. At first, it was frustrating — Instagram looked insane on it (it has since been updated to fill the screen slightly more) — but it quickly felt like salvation. I was less compelled to open apps that consumed my time. When using the front screen, I did my business and got out, like we used to on our phones. At times, I wished Apple would release a single-screen iPhone with just this smaller, shorter display.

But it’s not really about the exterior display, is it? Opening the iPhone Duo is both magical and hilarious. Foldable Android phones have been around for years, but outside of Billy Evans in the second half of You Can See Everything, you rarely see them unfolded. Apple has applied its typical UI gloss, with animations that almost flirtatiously coax you into opening it up. Inside, the screen has a matte “nano-texture” coating, which felt foreign to someone who has never used a screen protector. Most Android foldables feels plasticky and cheap, and while the Duo’s interior display doesn’t feel as premium as the exterior glass, it does feel like an upgrade. Plus the matte finish has the added benefit of hiding the crease in most lighting situations. But, to be clear, it’s still there, and I don’t get the hubbub. Of course it has a crease — it folds!

I’ve been using the Duo in semi-secret, since it’s a loaned-out reviewer’s unit — and when you do use it in the wild, a million people ask to touch it. Between that and my lifelong fear of being seen as a public iPad person, I mostly unfolded it at home at first, just like my beloved iPad. I thought, What a waste! What’s the point of carrying around this humiliation machine if not to open it? I should just be using my iPad! Once I braved up and got over that, I found it remarkable to open up this thing on the subway. I felt myself whizzing through articles faster than on my phone, and I even re-downloaded the Apple Books app, flipped the phone horizontally, and read like I was holding a physical book. The matte display makes reading an even more natural experience, and the aspect ratio of the inside screen lends itself well to text. For my job, I end up reading a lot of PDF versions of our print stories, and opening them up on the Duo is a delight.

But most of my job here at New York is creating vertical 9:16 videos for our socials. The iPhone Duo upends my livelihood. While you obviously can watch vertical content on the iPhone Duo (and I have watched plenty in my time testing the device), it doesn’t feel natural. The form factor begs you to either communicate quickly on the front screen or lean back and consume on the inside screen. Before the Duo, I did not have the TikTok app on my phone — only on my iPad for dedicated scrolling sessions with my perfect algorithm. I re-downloaded it on the Duo, since I have been testing this device as a possible replacement, but I haven’t found myself watching it much. The displays are squarer than those on an iPad, and the black bars surrounding vertical content make it less all-consuming, less addicting. The device has given me a bit of an existential crisis about my line of work. (Will vertical video be dethroned if the Duo reigns supreme? Will we all have to pivot our pivot-to-video strategies again?) Using the Duo, you become aware of how much of our economy is built around the shape of our phones. 9:16 displays have been the norm for about a decade, becoming ubiquitous with the release of the iPhone X (coincidentally, the year TikTok launched). If we hadn’t spent the past ten years using vertical rectangles, what would our content landscape look like?

The device is not perfect — completely unoptimized apps end up as bad-looking blown-up iPhone apps, and those are the ones least likely to ever update; the selfie cameras are a noticeable downgrade from the Pro iPhones, and maneuvering it one-handed can be tough. One of the biggest flaws of this expensive device is how tough it will be to protect it. Apple provided me with two loaner cases — the $129 (ouch!) Smart Folio and the $79 (yeesh!) case. The latter is affixed to the device with adhesive and adds a considerable amount of bulk to an already-thick device. I have opted for the magnetic folio case, which works the same way as a classic iPad magnetic case, and is definitely not protective against a big fall. Using the case has been inconvenient in ways that are entirely my fault. Take the most horrible situation a New Yorker can be in: trying to find a Citi Bike parking spot when all the docks are full. It’s nearly impossible to get the front cover off the screen, unlock the phone (the Duo has Touch ID, not Face ID, which is an easy swap except in this instance), and use it one-handed. This, of course, is not a flaw with the Duo but a flaw with the organization of Citi Bike docks — and with me for trying to unsafely use my phone (briefly) while biking. The front cover also keeps you from seeing every notification that comes in, weaning me off my phone even further.

It feels silly to meaningfully recommend a first-generation $2,000 (oy!) device because it makes you use your phone less. Except it doesn’t. It makes you use your phone better. Sentiment toward technology is at an all-time low, and it’s only getting worse with AI. The Duo is both a taste of the future and extremely retro. Its physical hinge harks back to the satisfying click of an iPod click wheel, or whipping open a Motorola Razr. Taking selfies with the wide-angle camera and previewing them on the front screen brings me back to taking Photo Booth pictures at the Apple Store with my friends in middle school. It reminds me of a time when technology felt good to use. While the apps on the Duo are the same apps deteriorating society, something about them feels less corrosive here. It’s a similar feeling to the one I’ve created with my iPad mini at home, but the Duo unlocks it everywhere — including, if we’re being honest, the best-use case for an iPad: toilet entertainment. Public bathrooms are now fair game. For someone whose job necessitates an ungodly amount of screen time, that’s the real win. You’re less likely to keep doomscrolling on the outer display after replying to a notification, and whatever you’re doing on the inside display, there’s a finality to it. You close the device and put it away.

entry.title: Four Ways I’d Solve the Clothes Chair
entry.summary: Including a wall-mounted drying rack and a patchwork pouf to camouflage laundry.
entry.content:
Clothes chairs are an inevitability, much like death and taxes: Nobody wants one, but everyone ends up with one anyway — Bernie Sanders included. At its most essential, the chair is a rest stop on the way from the closet to the laundry bin, holding clothes that aren’t clean but aren’t really dirty (a state described as “clurty” by one of our respondents). From that toehold, the clothes chair takes on additional roles: dumping ground for fresh laundry, staging area for tomorrow’s clothes, a semipermanent holding area for garments without a clear home.

If the chair is universal, so is the fantasy of eliminating it — everyone I talked to for this article wanted it gone. But I’d argue that the clothes chair cannot be organized away; remove it and piles will emerge in its place. It performs an essential function, and if we accept that clurty clothes are part of life, we can treat them like part of a system rather than clutter. Below are four solutions to four very different clothes-chair quandaries. To find previous installments of “Clutter Clinic,” click here — and if you have a mess for me to fix, email a photo and a brief explanation to strategist@nymag.com.

Primary complaint: “I have a FreshDirect bag full of sweaters on the floor next to my dresser that are in that liminal space where you have definitely worn them but they are not yet dirty. I don’t want to hang them up or put them in a drawer.”

I am with you here — sweaters do not like being hung up (gravity puts stress on the fibers), and they take up a lot of space in a dresser. This corner is cramped at ground level but has plenty of space if you build upward. Why not add a bookcase just for sweaters? This accomplishes a couple of things — a case will contain the sweaters on three sides, keeping them from sliding around, and it will give you more storage space vertically. The sweaters are happy, the pile is gone, and you don’t have to hang them.

The cheapest option here would be a dinky medium-density fiberboard shelf from Wayfair, but next to your dresser, I feel you deserve real wood. Search for “unfinished wood furniture” in your area — I found these two shelves at Gothic Furniture, which has locations in Manhattan and Queens. They can be stained to match the dresser, or you can save money by handling the finish yourself (or leaving them unfinished). I’ve also included a similar shelf from Lowe’s that ships for free.

Facebook Marketplace and AuctionNinja are also essential stops; you can’t beat the quality-to-price ratio of secondhand wooden furniture. I love the carved details on this skinny shelf, and for more options, search “bookcase” and filter for location here.

Primary complaint: “I would love to not have a clothes chair because it’s visually unappealing but have never in my life been able to figure out a different solution. Sometimes I put my favorite clean clothes on there because I’m like, I’m gonna wear these ASAP. I want it to look more intentional, less like a person has died and evaporated there.”

This is such a pretty corner, and I believe we can sneak some clothes storage in here without abutting the closet door or making it look like someone melted. The plant is already anchoring this area, and more bulk on the floor cuts into your walking path — I’d suggest moving the entire clothes chair up, mounting a wall rack that can hold a few items and display tomorrow’s clothes.

One option is a dowel rack, which can be expanded or collapsed flat depending on what it’s holding. I’ve included a collapsible Amish-made wall dryer and two options from Etsy, one with lower and higher capacity. (If you don’t mind lower capacity, I also love this metal one from the former USSR.)

I also found this handmade walnut shelf from a furniture store in Ukraine, which has a towel bar you could drape a pair of jeans over and a shelf above for stacks of clothes. The dimensions shown aren’t quite right for the asker’s space, but the seller offers custom sizes via DM.

Primary complaint: “I pile my clothes everywhere, and I wear what’s on top of the piles. There’s a valet chair from Ikea with stuff hanging off it, a pile of clothes I mainly wear around the house, and a bag of sweaters that need dry cleaning. Almost everything in this photo is “clurty” (not clean but not dirty). I need to do a purge of things I don’t use anymore, keep up with the dry cleaning, and find places to put the clean clothes. Looking at it makes me feel gross!”

The challenge here is congestion — the clothes aren’t making it back to their homes, so the piles grow. I agree that donating unworn things is a good first step (if you’re in New York, try St. Mary’s Clothing Drive — you can schedule a pickup online, and it’s free). Then start putting everything away, but change the goal: Let yourself off the hook for clearing the piles today. Instead, tune into your reactions, notice where you feel stress and friction. Take those feelings seriously — write them down.

Maybe you hate looking for something in a dark closet or the feeling of forcing a drawer shut or not being able to see an important garment. Maybe there is not enough space to store everything. Then reset your space based on what you’ve learned about what makes you feel good. The key to organization is not self-discipline, it’s self-love; approach the piles with curiosity and they’ll take another shape.

Light has been really helpful for me, so I’ve linked a set of motion-activated stick-on LEDs above. Some other ideas: an atomic-style coat rack to keep the house clothes accessible, vacuum bags for storing clothes you don’t wear, under-bed boxes for less-worn clothes (I think of this as having an A team and a B team), very skinny clothes hangers to maximize closet space, and a wall-mounted pot rack you could use as a hanger for smaller garments or accessories.

Primary complaint: “I hate displaying any form of laundry in the open. I want a solution that hides the clothes so my chair can just be a chair.”

The clothes stick out on a spindly wooden chair, but I wonder if they would look less prominent against a textile. I found two ottomans that would do the trick, one made of denim, cotton, and linen and the other made of woolens (tartan and tweed) — the patchwork will camouflage the mix of fabrics.

If the goal is to hide the laundry, a mirror is as close to a disappearing act as you can get. There are three options below: an Ikea mirror with a clothing rack behind it that we spotted on Maryam Nassir Zadeh’s Instagram and two versions from Wayfair that rotate 360 degrees — one that hides a rack and shelving, the other with a full cabinet behind it.

entry.title: On My Mind: Redecorating Two Tween Bedrooms at Once
entry.summary: Plus eyeball jewelry and puffer-coat shoes.
entry.content:
Every room in my house is in some sort of flux. My daughters are 8 and 11 now, and figuring out how different spaces need to evolve as they get older has become something of an all-consuming logic puzzle. We live in the suburbs and have the luxury of multiple bedrooms, but until a few months ago, the girls shared one anyway; in July, we moved the 11-year-old into what we previously called the guest room but had kind of become a dumping ground for whatever didn’t fit elsewhere (we don’t actually host many guests). At one point I had grand plans of picking her up from a week of summer camp — which ended right before her birthday, with middle school on the horizon — and surprising her with a flashy home-makeover-show reveal. But in reality it’s been a series of half-measures, whatever we can get done and afford little by little. Finding good stuff on Facebook Marketplace and then going to pick it up takes time. And of course she has so many of her own ideas, as does her younger sister.

Untangling the two kids’ stuff has been tough. I obviously should have anticipated more of the arguments over what belongs to whom, and who gets to keep what, since peak sibling rivalry was one of the reasons for making the split in the first place. It’s like going through a breakup. One girl is happily still sleeping in the twin-size bunk bed they previously shared, surrounded by a bunch of books and toys that need sorting though and clearing out. The other is starfishing in the expanse of a queen-size bed that came with the place and peppering us with questions about when we’re going to get the rest of our own junk out of there, repaint, and put up shelves. Each has an ever-changing wish list full of new furniture and décor and will inevitably be getting bedding and home goods for Christmas. Parents who’ve done this before: Please, share your wisdom!

One of the first things we bought to help personalize the new room fast was this cat switch plate to zhuzh up an outlet that’s in a particularly visible and inconvenient spot.

Even though she now has an entire closet to herself, the 8-year-old has become obsessed with getting a locker like the one her sister has at school. We’ve been browsing Mustard Made because the colors are so good; she likes the double-wide Twinny in light pink, which will probably be easier and more versatile to organize inside, though I also see the appeal of side-by-side Skinnys in different colors. (Thankfully the brand has a sale is coming up.)

When my older daughter was an infant and we lived in a one-bedroom apartment, I bought an an oversize Miffy lamp that was cheaper a decade ago but a splurge nonetheless. We plunked it down on mine and my husband’s dresser, then newly cleared off to make room for a changing pad on top, and used it during nighttime feedings and diaper changes. It’s been around ever since, a softly glowing bunny beacon who these days always has necklaces and headbands looped around her ears. Neither girl wants to part with it, so the older one has requested this smaller version.

This cheerful yellow — and actually affordable — coat rack might be handy for the child whose wardrobe is 90 percent hoodies.

Both kids need new desks for doing homework, drawing, and crafting. They also both need bookshelves, storage for art supplies, and a place to display their favorite LEGO builds, squishies, and assorted mementos and trinkets. I’m all over the place between simple tables combined with modular drawers, desks that have built-in drawers and hutches, wall-mounted systems that will make better use of vertical space, sit-to-stand desks that will literally grow with them, neutrals versus bright colors, and trying to stick to a budget while also wanting to avoid particleboard and having regrettably expensive taste. (It doesn’t help that the closest Ikea is two hours away.)

The older kid needs a comfy place to lounge and read. I think she would absolutely lose it if we got her a papasan chair, but they’re kind of gigantic. I also think it’d be awesome to have a hanging chair or cocoon swing in one corner, but the layout of the room doesn’t allow for that and I’d like to be able to easily move it around. So I’m still on the hunt.

I am simply unable to resist an eye motif and will be adding these Grainne Morton studs to my Christmas list once I decide between a matching pair or singles in different colors.

My sister’s got a milestone birthday coming up, and I am currently hyperfixated on buying two of these incredible Emma Brooke googly eye charms for us to wear as BFF tokens. They com in sterling silver or 14-karat gold and really move!

I am attempting to DIY a squishy dumpling Halloween costume to wear when I volunteer for one daughter’s classroom party next week. Assuming one of these inflatable “body bumpers” will fit me, it could make a good base.

I previously had a tortiseshell case from Flaunt on my iPhone and loved the look of the squared corners until they started a hole in the back pocket of a beloved pair of jeans. Now I’m testing this case from Urban Sophistication that seems very appropriate for the change in seasons. It’s sadly not MagSafe compatible, but it is pretty comfortable to hold.

I tend to go full puff as soon as it gets even slightly cold, so these slip-ons are looking especially plush right now.

entry.title: I Know Which iPad You Should Get
entry.summary: I’ve tried nine models since 2012, including all the models in the current lineup.
entry.content:
Since the first iPad was released in 2010, Apple has come out with 45 models of its tablet, including versions of the iPad Air, Mini, and Pro. At least one product in the lineup changes every year, and it can be hard to figure out which one works best for your needs. Apple currently sells four iPad models, two of which come in two sizes. iPads with faster processors will be better for heavy tasks like video editing and will have better longevity than those with slower or older chips. But if you don’t plan on using an iPad as your main work device, you might consider a cheaper model with a screen that’s almost as good as the one on pricier models.

I’ve been using iPads since 2012 for taking notes in school, serving as my primary nonwork computer, and doing illustrations for my newsletter, among many other tasks. I’ve chosen different models depending on my changing needs and in that time have learned what the best-use cases for each iPad in Apple’s lineup are. Whether you’re an illustrator, photographer, or just a casual reader who likes a big, bright screen, there’s an iPad for you.

Update on October 21, 2026
Updated to the most recent models; updated prices and checked stock for all products.

The iPad Air, Apple’s mid-range tablet, has a powerful chip that can run all the apps most people use to get work done, plus its display and thin design make it an excellent tablet for watching videos and reading. It also has support for Apple’s Pencil, Pencil Pro, and Magic Keyboard, all of which expand the tablet’s capabilities to more robust illustration work and writing (Apple’s keyboard case is good enough for replying to all your emails, too).

The Air has a 10.9-inch display that’s just a tad smaller than the (smaller) 11-inch iPad Pro, but the difference is barely noticeable. Its display doesn’t have quite as fast a refresh rate, which is what makes things like video playback and scrolling look significantly better on the Pro, but you’ll only miss the feature if you’ve spent a lot of time with it. For everyday use, the iPad Air still makes videos look good.

On the other hand, the maximum storage for the Air is 1TB, while the Pro goes up to 2TB. Additionally, because it uses the previous-generation M4 chip, the Air isn’t quite as powerful as the Pro, with its M5 processor, but the difference likely won’t be noticeable unless you do a lot of resource-intensive work on your tablet (things like working on video projects with a lot of clips will take longer on a less powerful chip). Having an older processor does mean that the Air will probably stop being supported before the Pro, but Apple has a good track record of keeping older devices updated for at least a few years.

Apple also sells a 13-inch version of the Air that’s identical in all but size. Given its extra weight and larger footprint, it doesn’t work quite as well for in-hand usage, but the larger screen is better for taking notes, drawing, and editing photos.

My biggest gripe with the Air is that it doesn’t use FaceID for unlocking and security (only the high-end iPad Pro supports FaceID). Instead, it uses an older TouchID sensor, which works well but is not as convenient or as fast since you have to hold your finger on the unlock button for a second for it to work.

The top-of-the-line iPad is great as a laptop replacement or as a more powerful tool for heavy video and image work. The latest model is equipped with Apple’s M5 chip, and the company’s most powerful tablet to date. That won’t make a difference for things like checking email or working in Google Docs, but the extra power will come in handy if you’re using this as your daily driver, and the Pro will get updates for longer than the Air given its newer processor.

The 11-inch model is slightly larger and wider than the Air, but it’s not enough of a difference to be a dealbreaker, and both weigh about a pound. Compared to the Air, the Pro’s display has slightly higher resolution, double the brightness, and double the refresh rate (and on the top-end models, you get the option of a nano-texture surface). That makes the Pro superior for editing videos and doing illustration work: the screen feels more responsive when you’re drawing with a stylus, but even just for watching movies and browsing the web, this display looks better.

Like the Air, the Pro supports both the Apple Pencil and the Pencil Pro and the Magic Keyboard, though the latest Pro models have an updated keyboard with an aluminum palm rest. These accessories are quite pricey, and these iPads start at well over $1,000 already, at which point you could also consider buying a MacBook. The newer M5 processor will provide more longevity than the Air’s M4 chip, but even so, there are similarly priced MacBooks that can do more simply because the professional app ecosystem is more mature, and Mac apps can access more system utilities than iOS permits. You can also connect more external displays to a MacBook than an iPad, which may make a difference depending on your office setup.

If none of that matters and you want the most powerful iPad that’ll work for years to come, get the iPad Pro. The 11-inch model’s screen is a bit small for illustration work, though I’ve been able to make it work just fine. On the other hand, it’s portable and light, so it’s easy to hold when you just want to read or play a game, and even with the Magic Keyboard attached, your bag won’t feel too heavy with it in tow.

If you take a lot of notes or doodle a lot on your iPad, get the 13-inch iPad Pro. It gives you significantly more real estate for using the Apple Pencil (plus about a quarter pound more weight). I had an older version of this size Pro, and I still miss the extra space when I’m drawing in ProCreate, even though its extra heft is significant. My hands got tired much faster when I held the 12.9-inch model for more than 20 or 30 minutes, and with the Magic Keyboard attached, it’s heavy enough to make you question whether you should just have a laptop instead. Paired with a lightweight case, though, this iPad can’t be beat for artists and students who like to take notes by hand.

No iPad is more portable than the iPad Mini. It has an 8.3-inch screen that’s packed into a body you can hold with one hand. It’s not quite compact enough to compete with a Kindle, but it’s still small enough to work as a travel reader and has many more capabilities beyond that. It’s by far the lightest iPad, and feels nice to hold — it’s my favorite tablet to use on the couch.

Like all other current iPads, the Mini works with the Apple Pencil, including the Pencil Pro. Unfortunately, it’s one of the only iPads Apple sells that doesn’t have an M-series chip, so it’s significantly slower than most other models. That won’t matter for things like reading and web browsing, which is really what this tablet is best for, but since Apple only refreshes this line every few years, you’ll have to compromise on processing power for portability. And like the Air, this tablet uses TouchID for security instead of FaceID.

According to Strategist senior editor Winnie Yang, “the best iPad to get a kid is a hand-me-down.” But if you don’t have an extra tablet laying around, Apple’s entry-level iPad is a perfectly fine tablet that’s notably cheaper than the other models. That’s mostly because it runs on a much slower chip, in this case the A16, and Apple’s A-series processors aren’t anywhere near as powerful as the M-series — it’s really best for light tasks like watching YouTube videos and playing games like Minecraft.

There are a few other compromises. Its screen doesn’t have an anti-reflective coating like all of the other iPads, for one thing. And the keyboard case for this iPad just isn’t as good as the one for the Air or Pro. Unlike the Magic Keyboard, which uses a laptop-like hinge to adjust the iPad’s viewing angle, the Magic Keyboard Folio for the iPad uses an adjustable stand on the back of the case. You can’t use it on your lap as easily as you can the Magic Keyboard, since it doesn’t have one solid base, but it works fine on a flat surface.

entry.title: I’m on the Boatneck Boat
entry.summary: It’s my new neckline of choice.
entry.content:
I became a certified boatneck truther over the summer after buying two (now unfortunately mostly sold-out) tees during a really good sale at Kotn. And perhaps it’s confirmation bias, but it feels like the neckline is everywhere right now. It’s a classic transitional-weather piece for fall: Obviously, you don’t want to bundle up with a turtleneck just yet, but it’s getting a bit too cold to be exposing your entire neck in a scoop-neck situation. The boatneck hits that perfect mix of a little sexy (exposed collarbone) and a little structured (see every marine top). Plus it’s a good excuse to wear a bra with cute straps.

The Goodwill gods really blessed me with this find last winter. Now I love it so much that I need to buy a few more colors full price. I own it in the ivory shade, which I use for all kinds of layering. It looks nice with a tank top or tee layered on top — a method that also shows off my tattoos a little. During chilly weather, I like to wear is as a whisper-thin (but surprisingly warm!) layer under a sweater. I always wash in a lingerie bag and air-dry it, and it’s held up very well with minimal pilling. It’s very stretchy; mine is an extra large, but I could easily size down to a large or even a medium.

Purveyor of fine sergercore attire Baserange obviously makes a nice boatneck. I purchased mine on sale at END. in hen yellow, which the brand no longer makes. It’s a bit revealing on its own, so if I decided to repurchase it, I would probably opt for black. While the fabric is fairly stretchy, I did have to size up a little to an extra large. Fair warning that the sleeves are extremely long (which is usually my preference).

After my dabbling with long-sleeve boatnecks, this was the tee that actually cemented my dedication to the cause. I own it in the blue-on-blue stripe pictured here as well as solid black. Normally, I like the neckline to be a little less dramatic; it often slips off one shoulder, which actually makes me feel very character in a mid-century film set in the French Riviera. The fabric has some stretch and is incredibly soft — par for the course for Kotn. And the banded hem ensures everything sits nicely and doesn’t expose my midriff too much.

It seems to be sold out in most colors and sizes, but sign up for the wait list; hopefully, it won’t be too long before the company brings it back! In the meantime, this tee from Gap is similar.

This Best in Class long-sleeve is nearly always on sale. It is quite stretchy and falls “between light- and mid-weight,” says creative strategist Carrie Carrollo, but the fabric still “feels substantial.” There was a point in time when she was wearing it weekly, and after every wash, it seemed “to only be getting softer.”

And I’m loving the sleeve length on this inexpensive tee from Gap Factory.

An option with a pocket, straight from the Strategist Fall 100.

A lot of alt-celebs — think Clairo, Audrey Hobert, Zoë Kravitz, Phoebe Bridgers — own this tee from Cleo. Writer Kitty Guo is also a fan: “It’s made out of a comfortable fine-rib cotton that sits close to the skin for a flattering, body-skimming silhouette with quarter-length sleeves perfect for showing off your bracelets,” she says. Writer Kat Gillespie also recently joined the camp: “I got this because the reversible nature of it really tickled me and I am always looking for a top that can be worn both day and night,” she says. “It’s the perfect top to wear when you don’t know what to wear. The other night I wore it to see David Byrne at Forest Hills, then attend my friend’s ‘bisexual awareness party’ in Bushwick afterwards.”

As our senior writer Liza Corsillo says, this splurgy option from Flore Flore is “the kind of T-shirt I imagine rich people have in multiples but I save for the days I want to look rich.” And the neckline “shows off a totally appropriate amount of clavicle,” she adds.

For a three-quarter-length sleeve that’s a fraction of the price, this one from Kotn fits the bill.

A little ruching at the waist takes the silhouette of this boatneck up a notch.

Same theory here, though the shorter sleeves make it better for date night.

It’s never too early to buy next year’s summer boatneck, especially when it comes recommended by two Strategist staffers.

Deputy editor Simone Kitchens liked the aforementioned tank top so much that she immediately purchased this version too. Ava Dunn, who manages a prop-rental studio in New York City, told us the baby-rib fabric is super soft and flattering. “It looks good on everyone,” she says. “I’ve convinced many friends to join me in owning every color.”

My two current obsessions — boatnecks and pointelle fabric — rolled into one.

The bell sleeves on this boatneck dress are a nice touch.

entry.content:
Long before skinny suits and barn jackets, J.Crew was known for its stylish, competitively priced knitwear. The venerable mall brand’s sweaters reliably offer better designs and more color choices than more affordable brands, while matching the construction and material quality one would expect from a blue-chip designer. I was reminded of this earlier this week, when I visited the J.Crew Men’s Shop in Noho to try every single sweater in the store.

I pulled 15 options over my head and each felt well made from high-quality materials — some even had an extra tag indicating the yarn’s origin, like the DOP seal on a fancy cheese or olive oil. A few sweaters were meant to be baggier, others were more tailored, but you can trust the designers to determine the right proportions for every silhouette. I am a true size medium in most tops, and I had no fit issues with any of the medium sweaters I tried. Overall, a handful of designs felt slightly more compelling than the rest, but I’d happily wear any of them again — with one minor exception.

For a brand so well known for rollnecks and cashmere, you’d think a cashmere rollneck would be a no-brainer, but it’s been about a decade since J.Crew last offered one in its men’s line. Having tried it on, I struggle to understand why it waited so long. Like the classic 1988 rollneck, it has a curled collar, hem, and cuffs, but they’re rendered more subtly in heavyweight cashmere. Where the cotton original is proudly oversize and slouchy, the softer cashmere version is more fitted and versatile. It’s relaxed enough to pull over a collared shirt, yet slim enough to fit under a suit jacket or chore coat, and it looks just as good with stonewashed jeans as it does with a blazer and trousers.

In recent years, J.Crew’s heritage cotton crewneck has had a more casual raglan sleeve, but I prefer the more elevated look of the new version’s standard shoulder seams. I originally tried the medium but liked the large a bit better. The heavyweight cotton knit drapes so luxuriously; why not get a bit more for your money?

Let’s be honest, how often is it actually cold enough to wear a heavyweight wool sweater in New York? This new soft-washed sweater still has the shaggy texture, variegated coloring, and elegant drape of a classic Shetland sweater, but it’s much lighter and more breathable. It’s soft enough to wear over a T-shirt and has a wide neck opening that layers easily over a collared shirt. While the sweater itself is made in China, it is knit from Yorkshire-spun yarns.

The waffle knit of this raglan-sleeve cashmere sweater gives it a slinkier drape and a smoother, cooler texture for incredible next-to-skin comfort. It wears more like a long-sleeve tee than a typical cashmere sweater and moves exceptionally well. The cut is pretty tailored, with just enough room to layer over a button-up shirt, but the texture is so nice that I can’t imagine you’d ever want to do that.

This subtly cropped sweater combines the smooth cotton neck of a rugby polo with the warmth and reassuring drape of a heavyweight wool knit body. It’s thick enough that you won’t need a topcoat on most fall days, and it would pair well with light-wash jeans or carpenter pants.

This chunky Aran-style fisherman’s sweater from J.Crew’s heritage workwear line, Wallace & Barnes, is knit from genuine Irish Donegal yarns. Its vibrant emerald hue and chunky texture look even prettier in person. Sadly, it’s already sold out online, but you may still find it in stores.

Cotton gets you that chunky sweater look without the sweat-inducing heat retention of thick lambswool. It also takes dye more readily, so designers can achieve deeply saturated colors that really pop. This butter-pink cable-knit sweater has a yellow undertone that’s hard to see in photos but is really noticeable in person.

J.Crew’s reissue of this iconic sweater coincided with burgeoning ’90s nostalgia and the release of Hulu’s Love Story to create a rollneck renaissance that led even rollnecks from other brands to sell out for months on end. The hype has only recently settled down as supply has finally caught up with demand. With scarcity out of the picture, is this thing really worth it? I like the oversize fit, drapey material, and low price. But a sweater like this demands to be the centerpiece of any outfit it’s a part of. I bought one last year and haven’t worn it as much as I thought I would because it’s hard to layer.

J.Crew’s cashmere crewneck sweater has been one of the best values in fashion since it was introduced in the 1980s. It’s just thick enough to layer over a button-down shirt without looking lumpy, yet light enough to not feel stifling at an overheated New York house party in the dead of winter. It has a more elegant drape and drier texture than cheaper sweaters because it’s knit from finer Grade A fibers, which are more consistent and pill-resistant. And it comes in over a dozen colors.

In addition to all the great solid colore options, J.Crew offers its cashmere crewnecks in marled and patterned styles for an additional $20.

J.Crew’s cashmere V-neck is made from the same great material as its crewnecks. I appreciated that the neckhole’s proportions are perfect for layering over a collared shirt. Sadly, even though V-necks are as big as they’ve ever been, this one only comes in ho-hum black, navy, and gray.

In addition to looking nice, this cable-knit cashmere is a bit thicker and warmer than its flat counterparts. It’s also more expensive. That said, it’s still a lot less than the similar Polo Ralph Lauren cashmere cable-knit. The Polo comes in more colors, but the J.Crew is the better value.

I loved the dry texture of this waffle-knit cashmere polo but ultimately preferred how it looked on the more casual, raglan-sleeve crewneck.

I’m not dogmatic about men’s clothing styles — I actually quite like J.Crew’s new line of cotton-collared wool rugby sweaters as a sort of two-great-tastes-that-taste-great-together mash-up — but adding a cable-knit pattern to the mix crosses into clothing design Mad Libs territory.
